13097-lives-of-the-most-remarkable-crimi:
Edited by Arthur L. Hayward, this huge collection reprints lives of criminals condemned and executed for murder, highway robbery, housebreaking, coining, and other offenses, first published in 1735. Its sources are original papers and authentic memoirs, drawn from the Newgate Calendar tradition. A frontispiece shows a highway murder on Hounslow Heath, with two highwaymen dangling from a gallows.

Volume one runs from Jane Griffin and John Trippuck through Walter Kennedy, Matthew Clark, and scores more. One condemned man, at peace after long confinement, rises at the gallows to urge the crowd to learn from his end. A woman thief, pressed to speak truth at her death, admits her tricks yet disputes a witness. The book is grim, moralizing, and rich in eighteenth-century crime detail.
17587-field-hospital-and-flying-column:
Violetta Thurstan, an English nursing sister, wrote this journal of a field hospital and flying column in Belgium and Russia, published in London and New York in 1915 by G. P. Putnam's Sons, first impression April 1915. Thurstan begins with a torchlight tattoo on Salisbury Plain, held on a breathless July evening when the peace of Europe was trembling.

Chapters run from the beginning of it all through trenches at Radzivilow, with an index closing the volume. Readers get a nurse's first-hand account of war medicine on two fronts, vivid and unsparing. The book suits readers of Great War nursing and of women's war writing.
18079-autumn:
Robert Nathan wrote Autumn in 1921, issued in New York by Robert M. McBride and Company, dedicated to D. M. N. and Herbert Feis. Nathan sets his novel in Hillsboro, a village where church bells ring over ripening fields.

Chapters run from Mrs. Grumble and school letting out to the Barlys, Mr. Jeminy building a house of boxes, rain, harvest, and the fair. The schoolmaster leaves Hillsboro, his work seemingly at an end, yet he is sought after all. Nathan writes with quiet, pastoral grace. It is a gentle, autumnal novel, full of village life and small, true feeling.
1814-the-agony-column:
Earl Derr Biggers, later famous for Charlie Chan, sets this light thriller in a baking New York summer two years before the telling, when the city felt like an anteroom of torture. A man answers a newspaper agony column advertisement and finds himself drawn into a tangle of mistaken identity and threats, including a servant named Walters who is taken aback by what happens.

The story moves fast, with letters tossed into waste-baskets and apologies offered too late. Biggers keeps the tone comic even as the danger grows. The book shows the future Chan author already skilled at the puzzle plot: a small ad and a wrong step. A hero must talk his way out of trouble he did not seek.
30508-the-instruction-of-ptah-hotep-and-:
Battiscombe G. Gunn translates two ancient Egyptian instructions in The Wisdom of the East series, published in London in 1906 and billed as the oldest books in the world. An introduction opens the volume, followed by the Instruction of Ptah-Hotep and the Instruction of Ke'gemni.

An appendix adds the Instruction of Amenemhe'et, plus an explanation of names and a bibliography. Gunn renders the texts from Egyptian into clear English, with notes for a general reader. The book offers early wisdom literature on conduct, speech, and rule, in a compact form that lets modern readers meet voices from the ancient Nile valley.
autumn:
Robert Nathan published this gentle novel with McBride of New York in 1921. Hillsboro, a farming village, turns toward harvest as church bells ring across ripening fields. Mrs. Grumble, the Barly family, and Mr. Jeminy, who builds a house out of boxes, people the opening chapters. A schoolmaster serves the village school while the year ripens around him.

Rain, the harvest, and a county fair carry the middle of the book. Old men trade memories of the last corn-husking before the war, when Anna Barly and Alec Stove lost themselves in the woods. Then the schoolmaster leaves Hillsboro, his work seemingly at an end — but he is sought after all, and found in good hands. Nathan writes a quiet pastoral about a village judging, too late, what its teacher was worth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-column:
Thomas Poole's entry defines a column as a round pillar or many-sided prism. Its body, reeded or fluted, stands near cylindrical and bears another body upright. Its chief part is the long shaft, set vertical on a molded base called the stylobate. A bulky mass, the capital, crowns the shaft. Columns take names from their style: Hindu, Egyptian, Grecian, Roman, and Gothic. In classic building they also take their order's name, such as Doric, Ionic, Composite, or Tuscan.

Position and form give more names. Attached, or engaged, columns join a wall, jutting out by half or more of their bulk. Cabled columns fill their flutings with cable work to a third of the height. Carolitic shafts wear foliage. Egyptian and Greek Doric columns had no bases, though capitals are universal. In Greek and Roman work proportions stay fixed. Modern use extends the term to iron or wood supports.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hymn:
A hymn comes from the Latin hymnus and Greek hymnos, from a verb meaning to sing. In ancient pagan literature a hymn was a prize song to gods or heroes, sung to the cythara. It first used epic measure, like the oldest hymn to Delphic Apollo, and later distichs or the refined lyric measures of Alcaeus, Anacreon, and Pindar.

In Christian literature the noun appears in only two New Testament passages, Ephesians and Colossians, together with psalms and spiritual canticles. The verb appears in Matthew, Mark, Acts, and Hebrews. Despite many attempts at definition, exegetes find it hard to say how far psalms, hymns, and spiritual canticles differ. Psalms belong to David, yet by content they may count as spiritual canticles, and by fitness for singing as hymns.
field-hospital-and-flying-column:
Thurstan keeps a war journal in Field Hospital and Flying Column, printed in 1915. Violetta Thurstan was an English nursing sister. Her book bears that plain stamp: the journal of a sister who served in Belgium and in Russia. It takes the reader with her party from the first days of the Great War.

The sampled pages find her group in Germany, on its way east. Crowds on a Hamburg platform jeered at the party and made coarse remarks. The women feared most for the men with them, about fifteen doctors and dressers, who might be seized at one loose word. Guards shut the party in a waiting room, and waiters near threw their bread and cold meat at them. A kind act from a young stranger, she says, made up for it all.
lives-of-the-most-remarkable-criminals-w:
Arthur L. Hayward edited these criminal lives from a 1735 collection. Original papers and authentic memoirs supplied the accounts. A Hounslow Heath highway murder illustrates the frontispiece. The victim is strangled while highwaymen dangle from a nearby gallows.

Contents name dozens of condemned murderers, robbers, and coiners. Jane Griffin leads a parade of forgotten offenders. Captains Massey, Roche, and Stanley bring military crime in. The volume descends from the old Newgate Calendar tradition. William Colthouse, John Thomson, and Thomas Reeves crowd the contents. Highway, housebreaking, and coining offences dominate the calendar's crimes.
nasa-tm-19700023619-vibration-tolerance-:
Richard R. Secunde and Arthur G. Birchenough of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in June 1970. It tests how much shaking a mercury-column coulometer can stand. A coulometer of this kind measures electric charge by tracking a moving mercury column.

The device was put through the vibration tests set for SERT II spacecraft parts. It also faced a standard military vibration scan, and it survived both, the authors state. Its electrical resistance dropped while it shook. Its core job, adding up charge over time, was not harmed by the tests. That made it fit for flight on the SERT II craft.
the-agony-column:
Earl Derr Biggers wrote The Agony Column, a mystery novel that opens in London in the last hot days of peace. Chapter one looks back two years to a July when the great city baked in fierce heat.

That heat, the narrator says, now reads like a warm-up for the hell of the Great War soon to break. Americans crowd the soda bar near the Hotel Cecil, while the English cool off with quarts of hot tea in Piccadilly tea shops. On Friday, July 24, 1914, Geoffrey West leaves his Adelphi Terrace rooms for breakfast at the Carlton. Readers get a murder linked to the personal ads — the agony column — of a London paper, on the eve of war.
